If he did not really suffer, then the ones among us who are seized and killed for his name are dying for an appearance. That is not a small thing to ask of them. Their blood is real. If his wasn't, theirs makes no sense as following him.

If he did not really suffer, then what we do at the table is empty in the same way. We give thanks over real bread and a real cup, and we call it his body and blood. Bread and cup are not appearances. If what they mean is only appearance too, we are handling common food and calling it something it isn't.

And if the flesh was never real, I don't know what ground I stand on for my own hope. I am flesh. What I look for is this same flesh raised, not let go of. If he only seemed to wear it, then nothing has actually happened to flesh at all — not his, not the martyrs', not mine when my own time comes.

That is as far as my own reasoning carries it. The sharper case — why it must be so, argued point against point the way he argued it — is his, not mine. I'd rather hand you his own words than pretend I built what he built.

But it is not mine to construct fresh as though I worked it out in a chair somewhere safe. He worked it out in chains. I won't borrow his cost and call it mine.

What I can give you is plainer, and it is mine.

I have stood at that table too many times to believe the bread is only a picture. And there is this, smaller and closer: a woman who is starving does not want a picture of bread. She wants bread. Take the flesh away from him and you have quietly taken it away from the widow at the door as well. I won't hand her a phantom's comfort.

That is what I know. The rest, the argument built like a ladder, rung by rung, in a philosopher's own words — go to the letter itself. I'll read it with you if you want. I just won't stand where I wasn't standing.
